uncited: This method converts voxel-space index bounds (defined by minimum and maximum coordinates along the $i$, $j$, and $k$ axes) into world-space clipping planes compatible with volume rendering pipelines.
It solves the problem of aligning rectangular crop regions with the physical orientation of the volume data, ensuring that clipping boundaries respect the image's spatial transformation.
It differs from inverse transformation methods by explicitly constructing plane primitives from index bounds rather than transforming existing world-space geometry.
**Extract Rotation**: Retrieve the rotation component from the `indexToWorld` matrix.
- If the `indexToWorld` matrix includes non-uniform scaling, the normal vectors derived from rotating basis vectors may not be unit length.
This variant generates clipping planes dynamically based on user interaction or changing crop regions.
It follows the same core logic but updates the `ijkPlanes` input in real-time.
The key distinction is the continuous recalculation of the `indexToWorld` transformation if the volume orientation changes, or the re-evaluation of the crop bounds as the user drags handles.
It is chosen when interactive volume exploration requires precise, axis-aligned cropping in world space.
- **Time Complexity**: $O(1)$ for plane generation, as it involves a fixed number of matrix-vector multiplications and plane constructions regardless of volume size.
- **Memory Complexity**: $O(1)$, storing only six plane objects.
- **Limitations**: Requires access to the full index-to-world transformation matrix; assumes the clipping region is axis-aligned in index space.
- **When to use**: When cropping a volume based on voxel indices but needing the clip boundaries to align with the world coordinate system.
- **When not to use**: When the clipping region is defined in world space directly (use inverse transformation) or when the volume has no spatial transformation (identity matrix).
This method is commonly used in web-based volume rendering applications using VTK.js.

It bridges the gap between logical voxel indices and physical world coordinates, enabling intuitive cropping interfaces where users define regions in index space but the renderer operates in world space.
It is part of the broader set of coordinate transformation techniques used in medical imaging and scientific visualization.
